title: Urban water affordability crisis exacerbated by climate change
methods: stochastic weather generation with CMIP6 anomalies
Pywr water resources system simulation (linear programming)
infrastructure financing and cost-of-service rate design (AWWA M1)
discrete/continuous choice econometric water demand model
data_sources: Santa Cruz Water Department monthly billing records (proprietary)
County of Santa Cruz Assessor's Office property and tax database
Santa Cruz 2020 Urban Water Management Plan
USGS gauge San Lorenzo River at Big Trees
Zenodo stochastic flow and weather data (10.5281/zenodo.18752509)

data_scope.spatial_coverage: single city case study - Santa Cruz, California (Santa Cruz Water Department service area, ~96,000 residents)
data_scope.supply_context: ~95% locally sourced surface water; single Loch Lomond Reservoir sized for about one year of supply; limited over-year storage
data_scope.billing_period: January 2009 - December 2021 (all active SCWD accounts; proprietary, Stanford IRB eProtocol 63914)
data_scope.household_unit: single-family residential accounts only; multifamily homes are master-metered and structurally absent
data_scope.income_data: block-group ACS 2019 5-year estimates + PUMS 2015-2019; household income imputed by regression and quantile mapping onto 16 ACS income bins
data_scope.climate_simulations: 50-year stochastic simulations driven by CMIP6 anomalies; mean precipitation x0.6-x1.2, precipitation CV x1.0-x1.2, temperature +0.0 to +5.0 C; treated as stationary
data_scope.figure_level_sample_sizes: up to n ~ 3.42e9 household-month affordability values pooled across all climate simulations (Fig. 3)
data_scope.infrastructure_options: five options, 0.5-4 MGD: two water transfers, aquifer storage and recovery, direct potable reuse, desalination
data_scope.not_reported: total number of stochastic simulations executed; number of ROF look-up-table runs (stated only as 'hundreds of 2-year simulations'); total affordability population beyond the 21,370 simulated single-family accounts

core_conclusion: Climate adaptation that preserves water supply reliability can undermine affordability. Using a coupled climate-supply-financing-rate-demand framework in Santa Cruz, California, climate change alone could nearly double median monthly water bills by mid-century (US$64 to US$120 under a dry, hot climate) and push an additional 7-16% of households above the EPA 2.5%-of-income affordability threshold (19% today to 26% under a moderate climate and 35% under a dry climate). Low-income median burdens rise from 3.9% to 7.3% and 90th-percentile low-income burdens from 16% to 30% of income. Under prevailing US rate-funded financing, reliability and affordability trade off directly, and the magnitude is locally contingent, requiring city-scale assessment.
why_it_matters: First framework to close the loop from climate stress through utility adaptation decisions, infrastructure financing and rate design to household-level affordability with demand feedbacks. It reframes adaptation as a distributional problem, sets a policy threshold at which utility-funded assistance becomes infeasible and state/federal intervention is required, names the mechanism behind affordability hotspots (supply vulnerability, exhausted conservation options, costly supply alternatives, rate-design constraints such as Proposition 218, income inequality), and quantifies the reliability-affordability Pareto frontier explicitly.
why_nature: Isolates a policy-generated sustainability trade-off in which successful physical adaptation transfers cost onto the least able to pay; contributes a re-parameterizable framework rather than a single case result; integrates stochastic climate generation, hydrology, multi-objective infrastructure optimization, municipal finance and microeconometric demand estimation; is directly translatable into financing, cross-subsidization and assistance policy; treats uncertainty rigorously and bounds its own generalization claim; deposits non-proprietary data and code on Zenodo.
added_value_to_my_research: Explainable surrogate of the coupled simulator -> national utility-service-area affordability hotspot screening
Learned adaptive planning policy with affordability in the objective -> financing-aware extension of my EV-charging equity-vs-efficiency optimization
Spatial microsimulation + dasymetric income surface -> recovers the missing renter/multifamily population, same coverage gap as in health-access data
Affordability ratio coupled to health-response layer -> environmental determinant of health with a modellable spatial exposure pathway
Agent-based demand with ratcheting elasticity and displacement -> corrects the selection bias where harmed households leave and metrics improve
